grid.teamDesc: Cadillac Racing represented General Motors' return to top-level prototype endurance racing with the all-new Cadillac V-Series.R. The program combined decades of American motorsport engineering experience with global endurance racing ambitions, competing against the world's leading manufacturers in the Hypercar category. Backed directly by Cadillac and operated with factory support, the team quickly established itself as a serious challenger for podiums and victories in the FIA World Endurance Championship.

The #3 Cadillac V-Series.R program spearheaded Cadillac Racing’s global campaign by combining an IMSA-proven foundation with factory-supported operation by Chip Ganassi Racing. Featuring drivers Sébastien Bourdais, Renger van der Zande, and Scott Dixon, the entry deployed its naturally aspirated 5.5-liter V8 engine to contend for overall podiums in the FIA World Endurance Championship's Hypercar class. You can read more about the team's international endeavors at Cadillac.

Ferrari AF Corse represented Ferrari's long-awaited return to endurance racing's top category after fifty years away from the premier prototype class. Partnering with AF Corse, one of the most successful GT racing organizations in modern motorsport, Ferrari developed the 499P Hypercar to compete for overall victories at Le Mans and in the FIA World Endurance Championship. The project instantly became one of the sport's most significant factory programs.

stories.title: A Tiebreak for the Crown: Fuoco Takes Spa as Buemi Survives Conway Thriller
stories.standfirst: A heart-stopping Ardennes finale ends with Sébastien Buemi and Mike Conway locked on 159 points, while Simon Mann takes LMGTE honors at Spa.
stories.body:
The mist that often blankets the Ardennes on a brisk autumn morning had long burned away by the time the green flag waved over Circuit de Spa-Francorchamps, leaving behind cool, crisp asphalt and a championship fight coiled like a spring. With 16 points separating Toyota Gazoo Racing teammates **Sébastien Buemi** and **Mike Conway**, and the crowning round reduced to an unforgiving 40-minute sprint, everyone in the paddock knew that perfection was the only acceptable currency. What unfolded across 18 frantic laps was something far raweur: a race dictated by heavy traffic, mid-race chaos, and a mathematical deadlock decided by the narrowest of margins.

From the drop of the green, Buemi looked to be executing a textbook title coronation. Launching cleanly from pole position in the No. 8 Toyota GR010 Hybrid, the Swiss maestro built an early gap, carving through Eau Rouge and up the Kemmel Straight with untouchable authority. By lap 8, Buemi held a commanding advantage, setting the fastest lap of the race at 2:07.541. Conway, starting from the outside of the front row, found himself bottled behind the rapid Ferrari 499Ps, watching his championship ambitions dwindle by tenths of a second with every passing sector.

## Mayhem at Minute 18 and the Toyota Heartbreak

Then came the 18th minute. As the Hypercar leaders began knifing through dense LMGTE traffic on the approach to the Bus Stop and along the run to La Source, the race turned violently on its head. A massive multi-car chain reaction in the GT pack triggered pure bedlam. Amid the melee, Buemi’s No. 8 Toyota was struck in rapid succession by Satoshi Hoshino’s Aston Martin and Claudio Schiavoni’s Porsche. The contact shattered Buemi’s rhythm, sending the pole-sitter tumbling down the order.

Pouncing instantly, **Antonio Fuoco** in the No. 50 Ferrari AF Corse slipped into the lead on lap 9. Conway, driving with ferocious urgency, navigated the wreckage to seize second. When the mandatory stops reshuffled the field—with Conway pitting on lap 11 and Dane Cameron briefly taking the front for a solitary lap—Fuoco resumed the lead on lap 13. 

Conway relentlessly hunted Fuoco over the closing six laps. The No. 7 Toyota carved Fuoco’s cushion down from 3.4 seconds to under a second, clocking a blistering 2:07.922 as he threw everything at the Ferrari’s diffuser. But Fuoco held firm, taking the checkered flag by just 0.889 seconds to score 26 points. Conway crossed the line in second, earning 18 points. Crucially, Buemi dragged his battered Toyota across the line in 11th place. While Buemi scored no finishing points, his pole position and fastest lap earned him two bonus markers, pulling him to exactly 159 points on the season—a dead heat with Conway. By virtue of his tiebreak countback, Buemi clinched the 2023 Hypercar Drivers' Championship from the jaws of absolute disaster.

## Mann Masters the Strategy in LMGTE

While the prototype title descended into Ardennes drama, the LMGTE division produced a masterclass in risk calculation. With **Nicky Catsburg** having already secured the drivers' crown for Corvette Racing, the spotlight turned to pride, race victories, and the final places on the championship podium. Pole-sitter Sarah Bovy looked utterly dominant in the No. 85 Iron Dames Porsche 911 RSR-19, commanding the opening 14 laps with a blistering fastest lap of 2:20.609. 

Yet behind her, **Simon Mann** and AF Corse rolled the dice. While the majority of the GT field banked on a splash-and-dash stop, Mann in the No. 21 Ferrari 488 GTE Evo committed to running the entire 17-lap sprint on a single set of soft tires without stopping. When Bovy ducked into the pit lane on lap 14 for a 40-second service, Mann inherited the point. 

Bovy emerged down in fifth and unleashed a furious recovery drive, clawing her way back to second by the final lap. However, Mann managed his tires with extraordinary poise, crossing the line 15.648 seconds clear to claim a brilliant season-closing victory. Thomas Flohr completed an AF Corse podium sweep in third, just edging teammate Luis Perez Companc, as the non-stopping Ferraris monopolized the upper reaches of the classification.

## Heartbreak and Resilience for Matt Stenzel

For **Matt Stenzel** and the Kessel Racing crew, the finale proved to be a cruel microcosm of endurance racing’s unforgiving nature. Starting from 12th on the GT grid, Stenzel drove an electrifying opening stint in the No. 57 Ferrari 488 GTE Evo. Carving past rivals on consecutive laps, the American had surged all the way to fifth in class by lap 7, putting himself squarely in contention to defend his top-five standing in the championship.

Just as Stenzel caught the leading pack, disaster struck in the 18th-minute carnage. Caught up in the high-speed accordion effect alongside Claudio Schiavoni and Christian Ried, Stenzel absorbed a brutal 2,349-severity impact that inflicted heavy suspension damage. Limping to the pit lane on lap 8, the team endured an agonizing 118-second stop to conduct emergency repairs and change tires. To compound the misfortune, Stenzel was hit with a stop-and-go penalty for speeding in pit lane, served on lap 10. 

Rejoining a lap down in 13th, Stenzel showed remarkable resolve. Despite carrying battle scars and managing ten track limit warnings throughout the sprint, his lap times remained impeccably disciplined, recording a consistency standard deviation of 0.381 seconds—far superior to the class average of 1.434. Although he was unable to score points, dropping him to sixth in the final standings on 64 points, Stenzel's season arc—highlighted by a magnificent podium drive at Fuji—cements a debut campaign filled with grit and raw potential.

## Champions Crowned as the Curtain Falls

With the engines cooling down in the shadow of the Ardennes hills, the 2023 Road to Glory campaign closes its books with undeniable drama. In Hypercar, Sébastien Buemi stands tall as champion on 159 points, sharing the total with a valiant Mike Conway, with Antonio Fuoco finishing third on 117 points following his heroic Spa triumph. Kévin Estre secured fourth with 97 points after bringing his Penske Porsche home in fourth.

In LMGTE, Nicky Catsburg wraps up a dominant championship campaign with 179 points, having led the field from the opening rounds. Simon Mann’s brilliant tactical win cemented second place on 130 points, while Proton Competition’s Harry Tincknell secured third overall on 90 points, holding off Luis Perez Companc (83 points) and Thomas Flohr (69 points). Stenzel follows in sixth with 64 points, capping a championship that delivered high drama, heart-stopping margins, and racing that will be remembered for years to come.

stories.title: Buemi Seizes Control in Catalunya as Catsburg Holds Off GTE Charge
stories.standfirst: Sébastien Buemi conquered Montmeló to overturn the championship lead, while Corvette's Nicky Catsburg survived a relentless GTE duel and Matt Stenzel staged a brilliant charge from ninth to the podium.
stories.body:
Under the warm October sun of Montmeló, the European Le Mans Series layout at Circuit de Barcelona stripped away every shred of ambiguity. There was nowhere to hide, no long straights to mask a flawed balance, and no forgiveness for tired rubber. With the 2023 Road to Glory campaign hurtling toward its conclusion, Round 5 was always destined to be the crucible where championship contenders either planted their flag or saw their dreams slip away. Over eighty punishing minutes, Toyota Gazoo Racing seized absolute authority at the top of the Hypercar pyramid, while the LMGTE class delivered an outright classic of cat-and-mouse endurance warfare.

## Buemi Outlasts the Prancing Horse

The tension at the head of the Hypercar field was palpable before the green flag even dropped. **Sébastien Buemi** had captured pole position in the #8 Toyota GR010 Hybrid by a hair, but when the field surged into Turn 1, it was **Alessandro Pier Guidi** in the #51 Ferrari AF Corse 499P who muscled his way into the race lead. For sixteen uninterrupted laps, Pier Guidi orchestrated a defensive clinic. Buemi stalked the red machine relentlessly, his front splitter tucked within two to three tenths of Pier Guidi's diffuser through the technical final sector, probing for an opening that never materialized.

The stalemate shattered on Lap 17 when both frontrunners peeled into the pit lane together. In the high-stakes dance of endurance pit stops, Toyota executed flawlessly. Buemi was stationary for 98 seconds before roaring down the pit lane, while the Ferrari crew took 101 seconds to service Pier Guidi. Those three seconds in the box proved decisive. Once the off-strategy Vanwall of Tom Dillmann and Loïc Duval's Peugeot cycled through their own service windows, Buemi emerged with clear air and the hammer cocked. Carving through backmarker traffic—surviving a heart-stopping 2,400-severity brush with Satoshi Hoshino's Aston Martin in the 66th minute—Buemi posted the race's fastest lap at 1:35.819 and built an unassailable margin.

Behind him, drama brewed for the remaining podium spots. Championship leader **Mike Conway**, who had qualified a lowly ninth in the sister #7 Toyota, mounted an extraordinary recovery drive. Carving methodically through the upper midfield, Conway stayed out of trouble until pouncing on an ailing Pier Guidi on Lap 44. The Ferrari’s medium tires had faded badly in the final stint, and Conway swept past into second, finishing 29.436 seconds back of Buemi. Pier Guidi only barely preserved third, clinging to the final step of the podium by just 0.446 seconds over a charging **Kévin Estre** in the #6 Porsche Penske 963. With a maximum points haul of 53, Buemi now vaults to the top of the Hypercar table with 157 points, deposing Conway (141 points) heading into the season finale.

## Catsburg and Tincknell: A Classic GTE Slugfest

If Hypercar was a display of calculated precision, LMGTE was pure, bare-knuckle competition. From the drop of the green flag, pole-sitter **Nicky Catsburg** in the #33 Corvette C8.R found his mirrors filled with the snarling nose of **Harry Tincknell**'s #88 Proton Competition Porsche 911 RSR-19. For nearly twenty-five laps, the gap between the two never stretched beyond half a second. Tincknell feinted to the inside of the Turn 1 chicane; Catsburg used the grunt of the American V8 to protect his exit.

Tincknell blinked first, stopping on Lap 22 for fresh rubber, while Corvette kept Catsburg out until Lap 24. That staggered timing briefly handed the lead to **Simon Mann**, who gambled on a marathon one-stop strategy in the #21 AF Corse Ferrari. Once Mann surrendered the point for his lone service on Lap 26, Tincknell swept into the lead, pulling a slender gap over Catsburg. But the Corvette ace was far from done. Bolted to soft tires, Catsburg reeled the Porsche back in, stalking Tincknell before launching a decisive overtake on Lap 38.

When both machines pitted for their splash of fuel and fresh softs in the final laps—Tincknell on Lap 41, Catsburg on Lap 42—the Corvette pit crew maintained their cool, sending Catsburg back out with a three-second cushion. He held firm to the checkered flag, claiming a magnificent victory by 3.352 seconds and swelling his championship tally to a commanding 175 points.

## Stenzel's Masterstroke: From Ninth to the Podium

Amid the titanic scrap for the win, the performance of the afternoon belonged to **Matt Stenzel**. Rolling off from ninth on the GTE grid in the #57 Kessel Racing Ferrari 488 GTE Evo, the task ahead of him was steep. Yet Stenzel drove with calculated poise and razor-sharp aggression from the outset. By Lap 5 he had scythed his way past five cars into fourth place, and two laps later he caught and dispatched Christian Ried to grab third.

From there, Kessel Racing pulled off a tactical masterstroke. While the rest of the field treated their first stops to full tire changes, Stenzel ducked into the pits on Lap 19 for fuel only, stopping for just 45 seconds before sprinting back onto the asphalt on his original mediums. He managed the wear brilliantly, pounding out consistent 1:46s in heavy traffic despite flirting right on the ragged edge of Montmeló's white lines—collecting thirteen track limit notifications across the race, though only one yielded an official warning point.

When Stenzel finally came in for fresh soft rubber on Lap 34, he rejoined in seventh. Unshackled on new tires, the #57 was a guided missile. Stenzel set personal bests, clocking a blistering 1:44.871—just half a second off the absolute class fastest lap—and swept past Thomas Flohr, Luis Perez Companc, and Simon Mann in rapid succession. Crossing the line in a lonely, brilliant third place just 11.463 seconds back of Catsburg, Stenzel secured 30 invaluable points. The haul catapults him from seventh to fifth in the LMGTE standings with 64 points, cementing one of the drive-of-the-day performances this paddock has witnessed all year.

## All Eyes on the Ardennes

With five rounds now in the books, the championship landscape has narrowed to its sharpest point. In Hypercar, the intra-team battle between Buemi and Conway is set for a dramatic conclusion, with sixteen points separating the two Toyota titans. Estre and Antonio Fuoco remain mathematically alive in third and fourth, but both require a miracle in the mountains. In LMGTE, Catsburg's 70-point advantage over Simon Mann leaves the Corvette squad with one hand firmly on the crown, but the scramble behind them is red-hot, with Tincknell, Perez Companc, and a resurgent Stenzel separated by narrow margins.

The stage is now officially set for the grand finale. The teams will pack their haulers and cross Europe for the ultimate test of nerve, speed, and endurance: the Fanatec Sprint at Circuit de Spa-Francorchamps. In the Ardennes, there will be no holding back.

stories.title: Heartbreak on the Concrete: Sebring Delivers a Sprint of Pure Drama
stories.standfirst: Under the orange glow of a Florida evening, Sébastien Buemi trimmed the Hypercar title fight to a single point as AF Corse pulled off a strategic miracle in LMGTE.
stories.body:
## Sunset Duels Over Sebring's Concrete

There is nothing on earth quite like Sebring International Raceway when the sun dips low across central Florida. The warm, thick autumn air hangs heavy over Hendricks Field, casting long, bruised shadows across the ancient fractured runways. For forty relentless minutes, the Mobil 1 Sprint asked twenty-four machines to dance across the fiercest bumps in global motorsport. What followed was a race of unsparing attrition, razor-thin margins, and tactical audacity.

From the moment the green flag fluttered into the evening sky, the Hypercar division became a private, high-speed duel between Sébastien Buemi in the No. 8 Toyota Gazoo Racing GR010 Hybrid and a predatory Earl Bamber in the No. 2 Cadillac V-Series.R. Buemi, having captured pole with a blistering 1:52.445, bolted into the lead through the punishing arc of Turn 1. Yet Bamber refused to yield an inch. Stalking the Toyota’s rear wing, the Cadillac trailed by a breathless six-tenths through the opening ten laps, the thunderous American V8 reverberating against the concrete walls as the two matched each other corner for corner.

## One Point Separates the Giants

When the frontrunners dove into pit lane on lap 13 for scheduled fuel stops, Tom Dillmann briefly inherited the lead for Floyd Vanwall before peeling in a lap later. When the order settled, Buemi held the hammer, but only just. Bamber rejoined a mere 0.4 seconds adrift, throwing everything into the braking zones of the hairpin and Sunset Bend. 

Buemi was ice-cold under relentless pressure. Clocking the race's fastest lap at 1:52.900, the Swiss maestro slowly built a tiny pocket of breathing room over the closing five tours. Buemi crossed the line to take a supreme victory by just 1.271 seconds over Bamber. Behind them, championship leader Mike Conway brought the sister No. 7 Toyota home in third, five seconds back, after a tidy drive from sixth on the grid. 

Further back, Antonio Fuoco and Alessandro Pier Guidi claimed fourth and fifth for Ferrari AF Corse, while Kévin Estre brought the No. 6 Porsche Penske home in sixth ahead of the factory Peugeots of Paul di Resta and Loïc Duval. Buemi’s sweep of pole, win, and fastest lap netted him 28 points, tightening the Hypercar championship to a single point: Conway now holds the summit with 105 points, with Buemi breathing right down his neck at 104. 

## Stenzel’s High-Wire Act and Heartbreak

If Hypercar was an exercise in pinpoint execution, the LMGTE battle was an emotional rollercoaster—and nobody rode the highs and lows more intensely than Matt Stenzel. Rolling off fourth on the grid in the No. 57 Kessel Racing Ferrari 488 GTE Evo, the American sim ace delivered one of the most explosive opening stints of the season.

While polesitter Nicky Catsburg controlled the early laps aboard the Corvette C8.R, Stenzel went on the offensive. Slicing past the Aston Martins and the Iron Dames Porsche, Stenzel hunted Catsburg down, erasing a three-second deficit within eight laps. By lap 10, the scarlet Ferrari was filling Catsburg’s mirrors, the gap shrinking to two-tenths of a second.

Then came the fireworks. On minute 18, as the two battled wheel-to-wheel across the unforgiving pavement, they touched hard—an 838-severity impact that left Stenzel nursing suspension damage. Unfazed by the battered handling, Stenzel threw the Ferrari down the inside on lap 11 to seize the class lead. For three glorious laps, Stenzel held the point, setting a personal best of 2:04.150 and showing legitimate race-winning pace while under intense pressure.

Yet Sebring gives no quarter to those dancing on the absolute limit. Stenzel had accumulated track limit warnings on laps 3 and 9, and on lap 13, another transgression pushed him over the edge. Race control issued a drive-through penalty on lap 14. Stenzel came in for fuel on lap 14 and served his drive-through on lap 15, losing 29 agonizing seconds in pit lane. From the euphoria of leading the race, he dropped to 13th before battling back to finish 11th. It was a brutal outcome after such searing speed, leaving him scoreless on the night and slipping to seventh in the standings on 34 points.

## The No-Stop Gamble That Shook GTE

Stenzel's misfortune opened the door for a strategic tactical masterstroke that stunned the paddock. Catsburg reclaimed the lead on lap 14 and pushed hard, but Corvette Racing elected to pit on lap 18 for fuel and fresh rubber, confident their blistering pace would see them through. AF Corse, however, had written a completely different script.

While Catsburg, Sarah Bovy, and the rest of the pack traded stops, Simon Mann in the No. 21 AF Corse Ferrari and teammate Luis Perez Companc in the No. 83 had committed to a daring zero-stop strategy. Starting from eighth and sixth respectively, the two Ferraris nursed their starting sets of soft Michelin rubber over the brutal concrete for the entire 40-minute distance.

Thomas Flohr temporarily inherited the lead on laps 18 and 19 in his AF Corse Ferrari before pitting on the final tour. That handed the point to Mann on lap 20. Catsburg charged like a demon on fresh softs, carving into the margin, but the checkered flag arrived too soon. Simon Mann pulled off an astonishing upset, leading only the final lap to take the victory by 5.466 seconds over Catsburg. Perez Companc held on valiantly for third, just three-tenths behind the Corvette, sealing an unforgettable double podium for AF Corse.

Sarah Bovy secured fourth for Iron Dames, while Christian Ried and Axcil Jefferies took fifth and sixth. PJ Hyett turned heads by snatching the class fastest lap (2:03.747) en route to tenth for Project 1 - AO. 

Catsburg's runner-up finish and bonus points lift him to 123 points, giving him a commanding 42-point buffer over Mann, who vaults to second on 81 points. With just two rounds remaining, the title fights are razor sharp. Next up, the paddock heads across the Atlantic for an 80-minute endurance battle at the Ten10 Motorsports Grand Prix at Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya.

stories.title: Conway Commands Imola as Catsburg Punishes the GTE Pack in Autumn Thriller
stories.standfirst: A masterclass from Mike Conway reclaimed the Hypercar summit at Imola, while Nicky Catsburg romped to an emphatic GTE victory amidst a ferocious midfield brawl.
stories.body:
The morning mist that clung to the banks of the Santerno river gave way to crisp, cool autumn sunshine over the Autodromo Internazionale Enzo e Dino Ferrari, setting an idyllic Italian stage for an hour of sheer endurance racing drama. Imola is a circuit that brooks no indecision. Its narrow ribbons of tarmac, violent kerbs at the Variante Alta, and unforgiving gravel traps demand absolute precision. Heading into the third round of the championship, the intra-team civil war at Toyota Gazoo Racing sat balanced on a knife-edge, while the LMGTE ranks braced for another bruising contest between Corvette muscle and European finesse.

## Conway Restores Order in Emilia-Romagna

Having surrendered the championship lead to his garage-mate Sébastien Buemi at Long Beach, Mike Conway arrived in Italy with an unmistakable air of unfinished business. From the moment the green flag flew, the driver of the No. 7 Toyota GR010 Hybrid stamped his authority onto the event. Conway darted clear into Tamburello, controlling the pace with surgical execution. His rhythm was relentless, clicking off typical laps in the 1:35.8 bracket and leaving the chasing pack to fight over scraps in his mirrors.

Behind him, Peugeot TotalEnergies mounted their most complete performance of the campaign. Paul di Resta, piloting the wingless No. 93 Peugeot 9X8, shadowed the leading Toyota through the opening salvo, keeping Conway honest and maintaining a comfortable buffer over the pursuing Ferrari of Antonio Fuoco. When the pit window opened on lap 15, Conway opted for a thorough service with fresh rubber and fuel, momentarily handing the lead to Tom Dillmann in the Floyd Vanwall. Once Dillmann completed his own tour through the lane a lap later, normal service resumed.

Conway re-emerged in total command, expertly managing his second stop on lap 30 and taking the checkered flag after 36 laps with a commanding 15.355-second margin over di Resta. Fuoco secured a hard-fought home podium for Ferrari AF Corse, just 1.295 seconds behind di Resta, giving the passionate tifosi reason to celebrate. Kévin Estre salvaged fourth for Porsche Penske Motorsport, hauling the No. 963 across the line with the fastest lap of the race—a blistering 1:34.952—while teammate Dane Cameron followed in fifth. For previous points leader Buemi, sixth place proved a sobering outcome, shifting the Hypercar championship pendulum back to Conway, who now leads the standings with 90 points to Buemi’s 76.

## Catsburg Cruises While Midfield Carnage Ignites

If Conway’s triumph in Hypercar was a display of calibrated control, Nicky Catsburg’s drive in LMGTE was pure dominance. Lining up on the front row alongside pole-sitter Harry Tincknell’s Proton Competition Porsche, Catsburg wasted zero time muscling the No. 33 Corvette C8.R into the lead through the Villeneuve chicane. Once clear into clean air, the Dutchman was untouchable. Producing metronomic consistency, Catsburg checked out, banking the fastest lap in class at 1:45.671 and leading 32 of the 34 laps completed.

Behind the yellow Corvette, however, the race descended into an all-out, paint-swapping dogfight. Tincknell found himself submerged in a relentless scrap with Axcil Jefferies in the Northwest AMR Aston Martin Vantage. When pit stops cycled through around lap 20, Simon Mann momentarily led for AF Corse on an offset strategy, but Catsburg resumed his perch with ease after a rapid 60-second service. Tincknell eventually consolidated second place, nearly twenty-nine seconds adrift of Catsburg, while Jefferies held onto third to cap a composed afternoon.

Yet the real heartbeat of the GTE race lay just behind the podium positions, where four cars circulated nose-to-tail in an agonizingly tense sprint to the finish.

## Stenzel Digs Deep in GTE Four-Way Slog

Starting from eighth on the GTE grid, Matt Stenzel was in an aggressive mood from the outset behind the wheel of his Kessel Racing Ferrari 488 GTE Evo. His afternoon began in chaotic fashion on lap two, trading heavy paint with Michael Wainwright’s Porsche, an impact measuring 1,582 on the contact index that set a frantic tone for his opening stint. Stenzel kept his foot pinned, carving forward through the lower reaches of the top ten before another major collision at minute 16—a bone-jarring 2,144 impact with Satoshi Hoshino’s Aston Martin—threatened to derail his progress.

Undeterred by the bruising wheel-to-wheel warfare and flirting with danger by racking up 26 track limit warnings, the Kessel team played a tactical blinder. Bringing Stenzel into the lane on lap 17 for a rapid 53-second fuel-only stop, they avoided tyre change delays and leaped the Ferrari up the order as rival pit stops resolved. By lap 24, Stenzel was circulating as high as second.

As the stint wore on, the absence of fresh rubber began to tell, but Stenzel demonstrated gritty car control. Though Tincknell and Jefferies slipped through on fresher boots, Stenzel anchored himself squarely in the middle of a breathless four-car train. PJ Hyett in the Project 1 - AO Porsche and Iron Dames’ Sarah Bovy swarmed all over the Ferrari’s exhaust pipes through Rivazza and along the pit straight. Stenzel refused to crack, crossing the line in fourth position, just 1.212 seconds behind podium finisher Jefferies and barely seven-tenths clear of Hyett, with Bovy another nine-tenths back in sixth. It was a spirited, hard-earned haul of 18 points that propelled Stenzel to sixth in the championship with 34 points.

## The Championship Equation

With half the campaign now in the books, the standings have taken a dramatic turn. In Hypercar, Conway’s maximum haul of 40 points vaulted him fourteen clear of Buemi, while Antonio Fuoco’s podium keeps Ferrari in touch on 63 points. Cameron and Estre remain closely matched on 54 and 53 points respectively, keeping Porsche Penske very much in the hunt.

In LMGTE, Catsburg’s commanding win and 40-point collection gives Corvette Racing a suffocating grip on the crown, sitting pretty on 103 points. Previous Long Beach victor Simon Mann failed to score after tumbling to eleventh in the pit shuffle, remaining stalled on 56 points. Tincknell’s second place lifted him to third on 47, while Jefferies climbed to fourth with 37. With Stenzel knocking on the top five door just two points behind Luis Perez Companc, the mid-pack war is boiling over.

The championship now packs its freight and heads across the Atlantic for the brutal concrete slabs and unforgiving bumps of the Mobil 1 Sprint at Sebring International Raceway. If Imola was an exhibition of rhythm and resilience, Florida promises to be an outright war of attrition.

stories.title: Southern California Twilight: Buemi Steals Long Beach as Mann Masters GTE Chaos
stories.standfirst: Under the golden Pacific twilight, Sébastien Buemi turned late-race precision into victory while Simon Mann conquered an attritional street brawl.
stories.body:
The sun dipped toward the Pacific, casting long, amber shadows across the concrete canyons of Long Beach, but the evening air provided no relief from the brutal intensity of street racing. An eighty-minute endurance contest pinned between uncompromising concrete barriers is an unforgiving test of nerve. One slight twitch of the wheel or a lapse in focus around the Seaside Way fountain, and the walls take their toll. Round 2 of the championship delivered breathtaking drama, unexpected heartbreak, and a masterful showcase of composure in both classes.

## Buemi Strikes Late as Cameron's Dominance Unravels

For nearly the entire race, **Dane Cameron** looked entirely untouchable. Launching from the outside of the front row in the No. 5 Porsche Penske Motorsport 963, Cameron executed a brilliant opening move to jump pole-sitter **Sébastien Buemi** on the run to Turn 1. From there, Cameron settled into a relentless rhythm, clicking off pristine laps and pacing the Hypercar field for 44 of the 60 laps.

Behind him, Buemi refused to crack. The Toyota GR010 Hybrid stayed glued within striking distance through the first round of scheduled fuel-and-tyre stops on lap 24. While Tom Dillmann stretched his opening stint in the Vanwall to briefly inherit the lead, Cameron reclaimed control once the cycle leveled out. Yet the race swung on the execution of the final pit sequence. When Cameron dove into the pit lane on lap 48 for his second scheduled service, Buemi stayed out, extracting maximum pace before peeling in. Thanks to a razor-sharp 86-second turnaround from the Toyota Gazoo Racing crew, Buemi rejoined with superior momentum, took the lead on lap 52 as the alternative strategies washed out, and surged away.

Buemi punctuated his masterclass by posting the fastest lap of the race at 1:15.550, crossing the bricks 5.041 seconds clear of Cameron to bag a maximum haul of 52 points. Kévin Estre completed the podium in the No. 6 Porsche (+10.850s), holding off Round 1 winner Mike Conway in fourth (+11.322s). Round 1 pole-sitter Antonio Fuoco had to settle for fifth in the No. 50 Ferrari 499P, trailing by 13.912 seconds, while Earl Bamber took sixth for Cadillac. With that victory, Buemi vaults to the summit of the Hypercar standings with 64 points, dislodging Conway, who now sits on 50.

## Heartbreak for Iron Dames and Aston Martin

If Hypercar was an exercise in strategic precision, LMGTE was pure, unfiltered attrition. Axcil Jefferies gave Northwest AMR the upper hand in qualifying, claiming pole with a searing 1:21.276. For the opening 30 laps, Jefferies controlled the tempo with authority, keeping a snarling pack of Aston Martins, Porsches, and Ferraris in his rearview mirror.

Then came the pit-stop window, and the street circuit showed its teeth. On lap 31, proton Competition's Harry Tincknell saw his race end violently against the barrier, triggering a devastating DNF for the No. 88 Porsche. Jefferies also suffered on strategy, forced into a two-stop sequence that ruined his shot at victory and relegated him to seventh. 

That opened the door for **Sarah Bovy** and the Iron Dames. Wheeling the pink No. 85 Porsche 911 RSR-19 with surgical flair, Bovy took command on lap 37 and led 19 consecutive laps, looking destined to write championship history. But the streets of Long Beach rarely permit fairy-tale endings. Cruelly, with just two laps remaining, Bovy was forced into pit lane for fuel, only to suffer a terminal DNF on lap 56 that robbed the Iron Dames of a deserved triumph.

## The AF Corse Coup and Catsburg's Charge

Waiting to capitalize on the front-running chaos was **Simon Mann** in the No. 21 AF Corse Ferrari 488 GTE Evo. Mann drove an exceptionally measured race. Sticking to a disciplined, single-stop strategy on lap 36, Mann let the frantic battles ahead burn themselves out. When Bovy dropped out, Mann seized the lead with calm authority, guiding his Ferrari home to capture a stunning 50-point victory.

Behind him, AF Corse celebrated an emphatic team showing, with Thomas Flohr claiming third (+17.050s) and Luis Perez Companc taking fourth (+21.705s). The sole interloper on the podium was championship leader **Nicky Catsburg**. Starting way down in 12th on the GTE grid, Catsburg carved through the carnage with surgical racecraft in the No. 33 Corvette C8.R. His clinical drive earned him second place, just 14.167 seconds behind Mann. The runner-up finish nets Catsburg 36 points, keeping him atop the GTE table with 63 points, while Mann leaps into second on 56.

## Bruised But Unbroken: Stenzel's Gritty Point

Among the evening's most dramatic personal odysseys was that of **Matt Stenzel** in the No. 57 Kessel Racing Ferrari. Starting from 13th in GTE, Stenzel unleashed jaw-dropping early pace. Slicing through traffic, he set the outright fastest lap of the class with a blistering 1:21.830 and had climbed all the way up to sixth by lap 13.

However, dancing on the absolute limit along the concrete barriers carries immense danger. At minute 23, Stenzel suffered a bone-jarring 2,975-severity impact with the wall, inflicting heavy suspension damage. A lengthy 120-second pit stop on lap 17 plunged him to the tail of the field. 

Refusing to retire the wounded machine, Stenzel battled on. Even after absorbing two further suspension-damaging wall impacts at minutes 63 and 79, plus receiving 17 track limit warnings as he wrestled the car, the Kessel driver refused to concede. Crossing the line two laps down in 12th, Stenzel was rewarded for his sheer defiance with a hard-earned single championship point, taking his season tally to 16 points and holding seventh in the GTE championship. It was a bruised, battered evening, but Stenzel showed genuine fighting spirit.

The championship now packs its freight and heads across the Atlantic to the historic asphalt of Italy, where the rolling hills and deep curbs of the Autodromo Internazionale Enzo e Dino Ferrari await.

stories.title: Conway's Late Ambush and Catsburg's Masterclass Ignite Portimão
stories.standfirst: Toyota pounces late on pole-sitter Antonio Fuoco while Nicky Catsburg dominates GTE as Matt Stenzel storms from last to the podium.
stories.body:
The rolling asphalt of Portimão does not ease a driver into a new racing season; it throws them straight into the tumult. Beneath the crisp autumn sun of southern Portugal, where the dry breeze off the Atlantic cuts across the undulating curves of the Autódromo Internacional do Algarve, the curtain came up on the Road to Glory championship with an electric 40-minute Prologue sprint. With points instantly on the line and no room for early-season hesitation, the opener delivered sheer tactical tension across both classes, setting immediate benchmarks and serving notice of what promises to be an unrelenting campaign.

## Conway Strikes Late in Algarve Thriller

For twenty-two laps, Antonio Fuoco looked untouchable. Placing the scarlet #50 Ferrari AF Corse 499P on pole with a blistering 1:37.023 in qualifying, the Italian launched into a commanding opening stint, carving through traffic and dictating the tempo from the drop of the green flag. Behind him, however, **Mike Conway** was playing the long game in the #7 Toyota Gazoo Racing GR010 Hybrid. Starting from fifth on the grid, Conway methodically dismantled the deficit, picking off Earl Bamber and Alessandro Pier Guidi before stalking the leaders into the pit window.

When the front-runners made their mandatory fuel stops on lap 16—Conway stationary for 54 seconds, Fuoco for 56—the gap evaporated. Although Fuoco retained net track position once intermediate leaders Loïc Duval and Kévin Estre completed their services, Conway applied relentless pressure. Armed with the fastest lap of the race at 1:37.428 and clocking an unrelenting 1:38.513 typical pace, Conway hunted down the Ferrari and seized the lead on lap 23 with a decisive move. Taking the checkered flag by 4.670 seconds, Conway pocketed maximum race points and the fastest-lap bonus to leave Portugal leading the Hypercar standings with 26 points. Fuoco settled for second and 20 points after leading 20 laps, while Duval held onto a remarkable third place for Peugeot TotalEnergies (+16.842s), delivering a hard-earned 15 points in the wingless 9X8. Sébastien Buemi fought through to fourth in the sister #8 Toyota, narrowly fending off Earl Bamber’s Cadillac V-Series.R by five hundredths of a second.

## Catsburg and Corvette Command LMGTE

While the Hypercar fight went right down to the penultimate lap, the battle for the LMGTE victory was defined by sheer, unblemished perfection. Nicky Catsburg delivered a clinic behind the wheel of the Corvette Racing #33 C8.R. After planting the yellow machine on pole with a lap of 1:45.983, the Dutchman simply disappeared. Managing tire degradation with extraordinary mechanical sympathy, Corvette Racing chose not to stop at all during the 40-minute sprint. Catsburg led every single one of the 23 laps, turning identical laps like clockwork—posting a median lap time of 1:47.839 with an astonishing standard deviation of just 0.39 seconds.

Catsburg crossed the line 43.069 seconds ahead of the chasing pack, scooping all 27 available points for the win, pole, and most laps led. The battle behind him, though, was frantic. Harry Tincknell unleashed furious raw speed in the #88 Proton Competition Porsche 911 RSR-19, punching in the fastest GTE lap of the race at 1:45.323. Pitting on lap 20 for fresh rubber and fuel, Tincknell rejoined with sufficient margin to claim a clear second place, earning 19 points to open his account. Yet the true drama of the production-based class unfolded directly behind them in an astonishing scramble up the order.

## The Charge: Stenzel Scales the Mountain

The drive of the day belonged squarely to human contender **Matt Stenzel** in the #57 Kessel Racing Ferrari 488 GTE Evo. Starting from dead last in fourteenth after a troubled qualifying run, Stenzel faced a steep mountain on a circuit where passing requires absolute commitment. What followed was a breathtaking demonstration of racecraft. While rivals tangled or struggled for rhythm, Stenzel sliced forward lap after lap, cracking into the top ten by lap two and muscling his way into seventh before the halfway mark.

His march through the pack was anything but gentle. The Ferrari was pushed to the absolute edge, clocking an eye-opening top speed of 266.21 kph on the Algarve main straight—by far the fastest recorded in the GTE field. Along the way, Stenzel absorbed heavy contact: a hard hit (severity 901) with PJ Hyett’s Project 1 Porsche around the eleven-minute mark, and a massive collision with Hypercar contender Sébastien Buemi at minute 29.6 measuring a colossal 2312 severity as multi-class traffic converged into the heavy braking zones. Despite collecting a track limit warning in the heat of battle, Stenzel kept the 488 pointed straight.

Kessel Racing timed their strategy to perfection. Calling Stenzel in on lap 18 for a swift 39-second fuel-only stop, they avoided tyre changes and jumped directly ahead of the Porsche contingent—including Sarah Bovy, Michael Wainwright, and Christian Ried—when those squads took both fuel and rubber on lap 20. Stenzel cycled up to fourth, then picked off Luis Perez Companc’s non-stopping AF Corse Ferrari in the closing moments to secure a stunning third place. An eleven-position ascent netted Stenzel 15 championship points and a podium trophy that felt entirely improbable forty minutes earlier. Perez Companc held fourth ahead of Iron Dames driver Bovy.

## Foundations Laid for Long Beach

With the opening salvo concluded, the championship tables reflect a fascinating hierarchy. Mike Conway sits atop Hypercar on 26 points, flanked by Antonio Fuoco (20) and Loïc Duval (15), while Sébastien Buemi (12) and Earl Bamber (10) lurk within striking distance. In LMGTE, Nicky Catsburg’s imperious 27-point haul establishes Corvette as the early benchmark, but Harry Tincknell (19) and Matt Stenzel (15) have staked their claim as genuine title contenders. Next up, the field crosses the Atlantic for the grueling Beach Endurance at Long Beach, where 80 minutes on the unforgiving California street course will test these early front-runners against concrete walls that offer no forgiveness.

stories.title: A New Dawn Beckons: Inside the 2023 Road to Glory Campaign
stories.standfirst: Six rounds of relentless multi-class warfare await as the world's finest prototypes and GT machines prepare to battle from Portimão to Spa.
stories.body:
There is a distinct, electric hum that settles over the pit lane when a brand-new season waits on the horizon. The liveries are immaculate, the carbon weave unblemished, and the ledger entirely blank. Ahead lies the 2023 Road to Glory championship, a six-round tour across the globe that promises to push machines and minds to their absolute limits. Multi-class endurance racing is never just about ultimate single-lap pace; it is an intricate dance of traffic management, stamina, and strategic daring. With two distinct categories sharing asphalt—the fire-breathing Hypercar prototypes and the fiercely contested production-based LMGTE machinery—every corner will be an exercise in spatial awareness and calculated aggression.

With an escalating points structure awarding up to 50 points to winners in the grueling 80-minute long-distance bouts, and 25 points on the line during the frantic 40-minute sprints, championship momentum can pivot in an afternoon. Added bonuses for pole position, fastest lap, and leading the most laps mean every fraction of a second matters from the moment pit lane green lights illuminate.

## The Battlegrounds: Six Steps Across the World

The campaign opens with a fast-paced sprint at the Autódromo Internacional do Algarve in Portimão. The Portuguese circuit is a rollercoaster of undulating blind crests and plunging drops, where drivers must commit wholeheartedly without always seeing the apex ahead. From the Algarve, the paddock crosses the Atlantic for an 80-minute trial by concrete at Long Beach. Street racing in multi-class machinery is a relentless test of discipline; the seaside Californian course offers zero margin for error, where a brush with the wall can wipe out an afternoon's work in an instant.

Round three heads to historical sanctuary: Imola. The Autodromo Internazionale Enzo e Dino Ferrari is narrow, bordered by vicious curbs, and unforgiving of overzealous overtakes. Surviving the Italian test leads into a bruising 40-minute sprint over the notorious bumps of Sebring International Raceway under evening skies. The weathered runways of Central Florida rattle suspensions and shake loose any mechanical vulnerability. Spain's Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya hosts the penultimate round—an 80-minute tactical marathon where tire preservation around the abrasive sweeping bends will reign supreme—before the grand finale at the cathedral of endurance racing: Circuit de Spa-Francorchamps. The Ardennes forest will provide the ultimate dramatic curtain call through the sweeps of Eau Rouge and the Blanchimont flat-out sprint.

## The Hypercar Vanguard: Giants Collide

At the sharp end of the grid, the Hypercar division represents a breathtaking clash of philosophies. Toyota Gazoo Racing arrives with unmatched endurance pedigree, fielding the peerless GR010 Hybrids. The #7 entry anchored by Mike Conway, Kamui Kobayashi, and José María López, alongside the sister #8 of Sébastien Buemi, Brendon Hartley, and Ryo Hirakawa, set the gold standard in operational discipline.

Yet the Japanese powerhouse faces a red-liveried assault from Maranello. Ferrari AF Corse’s factory 499P prototypes—the #50 driven by Antonio Fuoco, Miguel Molina, and Nicklas Nielsen, and the #51 of Alessandro Pier Guidi, James Calado, and Antonio Giovinazzi—are poised to reclaim the Prancing Horse’s top-flight heritage. Porsche Penske Motorsport counters with the aggressive pair of 963 prototypes (#5 and #6), boasting established endurance stalwarts like Kévin Estre, Laurens Vanthoor, and André Lotterer. With customer entries from Hertz Team JOTA and Proton Competition reinforcing the Porsche fleet, alongside the roaring V8 of Cadillac Racing’s #2 V-Series.R, the avant-garde wingless Peugeot 9X8s, and spirited efforts from Glickenhaus and Vanwall, the outright fight will be a vicious, unrelenting affair.

## The Final Song of GTE: Pure Multi-Car Warfare

While prototypes hunt outright glory, the LMGTE field offers an intoxicating, elbow-to-elbow brawl that may well deliver the closest racing of the year. This marks the swan song era for the naturally aspirated shrieks and twin-turbo growls of pure GTE platforms, and the entry list is stacked with championship credentials.

Corvette Racing’s singular C8.R (#33), led by the ever-reliable Ben Keating and Nicky Catsburg, enters as an immediate benchmark on pace and operational consistency. Yet the Porsche 911 RSR-19 contingent is massive and lethal. The crowd-favorite Iron Dames (#85) lineup of Sarah Bovy, Rahel Frey, and Michelle Gatting proved time and again they can control a race from the front, while Dempsey-Proton (#77), Project 1 - AO (#56), and GR Racing (#86) bring deep technical experience to the table. Aston Martin’s trio of Vantage GTEs, headed by ORT by TF (#25) and NorthWest AMR (#98), are primed to exploit any high-speed circuit characteristics.

## Stenzel in the Spotlight: Kessel Racing’s Challenge

In the heart of this cutthroat GT arena sits **Matt Stenzel**, strapping into the cockpit of the #57 Kessel Racing Ferrari 488 GTE Evo. Stenzel carries both the pride and pressure of representing the Swiss-based squad, sharing the stable’s lineage with veterans like Daniel Serra and Takeshi Kimura. The 488 GTE Evo is a refined, beautifully balanced weapon, renowned for its stability under heavy braking and gentle tire wear, which should pay enormous dividends on long stints like Long Beach and Barcelona.

For Stenzel, the mission is formidable. Running against factory-backed efforts and elite GT privateers on a 90 percent difficulty benchmark leaves no room for hesitation. Survival through the chaotic prototype traffic while keeping the #57 machine glued to the rear bumpers of the Corvettes and Porsches will test racecraft and calm nerve alike. If Stenzel can combine opportunistic overtaking with disciplined tire management across the opening skirmishes in Portimão and Long Beach, Kessel Racing could quickly emerge as a genuine thorn in the side of the established favorites. The engines are warming in the garages. Road to Glory is underway.
